blocks.text: I take the liberty of expressing the following conjecture here. The words of the Targum on Spr. Salom. 27, 22, which in the Basel edition of the מקראות גדולות read erroneously בגו סיעתא ובאורדך and must read בגו סיעתא ובאורדך, are explained in various ways. Landau (s.v. ארדך) explains the last word by ארוד “wild ass,” which was used for grinding; Salomon Buber (in the מגד ירחים, 1st issue, p. 48) reads אסיתא (mortar) for סיעתא and ובמרוך (pestle) for ובאורדך. — The question arises, however, how the ו-copulativum is to be explained, since the text has בעלי and not ובעלי? I believe that the ו belongs to סיעתא, but has been corrupted from a final ך and drawn to the following word. I would read בגו סיעתאן באור דך. The second word is the Greek Σείσων [Seisōn], a vessel that is placed over the fire and in which beans, grains and the like are roasted; the translation of the verse would be: “Though thou bray a fool with a pestle in the pounding vessel over a bright fire, yet will not his foolishness depart from him.” — In any case Buber's explanation is simpler and more natural.
Nevertheless their claws were not allowed to be removed, because one should not torment even the wildest animal (ibid.); cruelty to animals was forbidden among the Jews already in the earliest times.

One did not wish to let either an obscene or an unaesthetic expression be heard in the presence of children, and therefore designated such a thing by the term דבר אחר; see E. Levita (Tischbi s.v. דבר). — The Pajtan (in the Sulat for the 1st Sabbath after Pessach s.v. אין כמוך) also calls the swine: חית נכר “the rooting animal”; cf. on this B. Kama 17b.
The פיסחקא mentioned in Gittin 59a Raschi explains as: acorns (גלנ"ש. Glands), which the swine eat; cf. §. 172.
On the well-known proverb: “The swine stretches out its (cloven-hoofed) foot in order to appear clean,” cf. Midr. Jalkut Schimoni part 2, fol. 115, d, and Rabba Bereschit fol. 72a.
In the Bible (Ps. 80, 14) the animal is called: חזיר מיער; the Pajtan (in the Jozar of the 2nd day of Pesach s.v. אפיק רנן) calls it: מכרסם מיער “forest-rooter.”

Here it says: פיל שבלע כפיפה מצרית והוציאה דרך בית הרעי, which is admittedly exaggerated, and therefore Reggio (Ozar Nechmad vol. 2, p. 201) rightly criticizes Maimuni (Jad. ha-Chasaka hil. Kelim cap. 1) for excerpting those words literally. Of the snake it is known that, after it has sucked out the food, it discharges it again whole through the anus; see Aristotle loc. cit. 8, 6, 1.

Pseudoraschi on 2. Chr. 9, 21 deviates strikingly from Raschi on the above passage. The former explains שנהבים as ivory and as the elephants themselves; Raschi more correctly, since the elephant is never called שנהב. On the etymology of הב see Rosenmüller (loc. cit. p. 104). — קפים, or קופים, the same translates as מעער קאצען “Meerkatzen” [guenons] without any reason. — Hitzig (Jesaias p. 643) explains שנהבים as “Nubian tooth,” by which the Hebrews sailing the Red Sea named ivory. Let it also be noted in passing that the use of the elephant in war is mentioned in the Sulat for the 2nd Sabbath of Chanuka with the words: לרכוב פילים כבהמתם. — On Ps. 45, 9 Raschi explains שן as ivory (איבויירא. Ivoire).
According to Midr. Jalkut Schim. part 2, fol. 97, d, the Reem reaches up into the clouds (heaven); cf. also ibid. fol. 154b.

The sense of that designation is only: the buffalo may be called ראם on account of its size; similarly the Greeks form the designation for the size of an object by compounding with βοῦς [bous], e.g. βούπαις [boupais], big boy, βούνεβρος [bounebros], big fawn, etc. see §. 409 at the end.
For the various statements of the Jerusalem Talmud about תחש see Appendix s.v. גלאקטינון.

Gräße has the following note here: “From what sources Alex. Dumas, in his tale The Marriages of Father Olifus (Tausend und ein Gespenst, the translation vol. 2, p. 167 ff.), relates of the fisherman Olifus of Monikedam near Amsterdam that in 1823 he married a sea-woman whom he had once caught in the sea, and begot five children with her, I do not know.”
Thus it is also said of the Liviatan in the Piut s.v. חשורת שי for the 2nd day of Succoth: לקשור לוית צלצל דנתי.

Indeed, before whaling became widespread, this animal was caught at 100 ells long and more, 50 ells wide and 30 ells high (Lindau: ראשית לימודים p. 34), which admittedly seems somewhat exaggerated.
